lessons.title: How the web works, and your tools
lessons.summary: What happens between typing an address and seeing a page, and the three tools you will use every session: a browser, a code editor and the browser's developer tools.
objectives: You will explain what a browser, a server and a URL are
You will open the developer tools and inspect a page
You will create, save and open your first .html file
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Install a code editor (VS Code, or an online editor if you are on a phone)
- Open any website, right-click, choose **Inspect**, and change some text in the Elements panel
- Create `index.html`, type a sentence into it, save it and open it in your browser
- **With an AI assistant —** ask it to *explain* a tag you are unsure of, then check it on MDN (developer.mozilla.org). Type the code yourself — copying code you cannot explain is not learning.

## Understand it

When you type an address such as `nextgengenius.ng` and press Enter, four things happen. Your browser asks a **DNS server** which computer holds that name, and gets back a number called an IP address. It then sends that computer an **HTTP request** — a short message that says "please send me this page". The computer at the other end, the **server**, answers with a **response**: a status code (200 means OK, 404 means not found) and the page itself, written in HTML. Finally your browser reads the HTML, fetches anything else the page asks for (pictures, CSS, JavaScript) and draws it on the screen.

Everything you build in this course fits somewhere in that journey. HTML, CSS and JavaScript are what the browser receives and draws — the **front end**. Node, Express and databases are what runs on the server and decides what to send — the **back end**. A full-stack developer understands both ends.

Your three tools: the **browser** (Chrome, Firefox or Edge) shows the result; the **code editor** (VS Code) is where you write; the **developer tools** (right-click → Inspect) let you look inside any page, see its HTML and CSS, and try changes live without breaking anything — reload and they are gone.

## Key words

- **Server:** a computer that waits for requests and sends back pages or data
- **HTTP:** the rules a browser and a server use to talk to each other
- **DNS:** the internet's address book: it turns a name into an IP address
- **Status code:** the number at the start of a response — 200 OK, 404 Not Found, 500 server error

## Read and watch

- [How the web works](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Learn/Getting_started_with_the_web/How_the_Web_works) — MDN Web Docs (Mozilla)
- [Chrome DevTools overview](https://developer.chrome.com/docs/devtools/overview) — Chrome for Developers (Google)
- [Getting started with VS Code](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/getstarted/getting-started) — Visual Studio Code (Microsoft)

lessons.body:
This lesson is about **39 freeCodeCamp steps**. Work through them in order — the steps build on each other.

## What to do

- Do the Semantic HTML workshop on freeCodeCamp
- Restructure your page so it has header, nav, main and footer

## Understand it

A `<div>` says nothing about what it contains — it is just a box. **Semantic** elements say what their content *is*:

- `<header>` — the top of the page or of a section: logo, title
- `<nav>` — the main links to move around the site
- `<main>` — the one main content of this page (only one per page)
- `<section>` — a themed group with its own heading
- `<article>` — something that makes sense on its own, such as a news post
- `<aside>` — related but not central, such as a side note
- `<footer>` — the bottom: contact details, copyright

Why bother if the page looks the same? Because not everybody *looks* at a page. A screen reader lets a blind user jump straight to `<main>` or list every `<nav>`. Search engines use the structure to understand what matters. And other developers — including you in six months — can read the code and see the shape of the page at once.

A good test: remove all the CSS. If the page still reads in a sensible order with clear headings, your HTML is doing its job.

## Key words

- **Semantic HTML:** using elements that describe what content is, not how it looks
- **Landmark:** a region a screen reader can jump to, such as main or nav
- **div:** a box with no meaning, for styling when nothing else fits

lessons.body:
## What to do

- Create a GitHub account (with a parent's permission if you are under 13 — GitHub's minimum age is 13)
- Make a repository called `my-first-site` and upload your index.html
- Change one line, commit it with a clear message, and look at the history
- **With an AI assistant —** ask it to explain a git command before you run it. Never paste passwords, tokens or keys into any AI tool or into a public repository.

## Understand it

**Git** is a tool that takes snapshots of your project. Each snapshot is a **commit**, with a message saying what changed and why. Because every commit is kept, you can always go back to a version that worked — no more `index-final-final2.html`. **GitHub** is a website that stores your Git projects online (a **repository**, or repo), so your work is backed up, shareable and visible to future employers.

The everyday loop has three steps:

```bash
git add index.html          # choose what goes in the next snapshot
git commit -m "Add contact link to footer"
git push                    # send your commits to GitHub
```

Write commit messages as if finishing the sentence "This commit will…": *Add contact link*, *Fix broken image path*. "stuff" and "update" tell nobody anything.

Two safety rules from the start: a public repository can be read by anyone in the world, so never commit passwords, keys or personal details; and commit small and often — a commit that changes one thing is easy to understand and easy to undo.

## Key words

- **Repository:** a project folder whose whole history Git keeps
- **Commit:** a saved snapshot of the project with a message
- **Push:** sending your commits from your computer to GitHub
- **Version control:** keeping every version of your work so you can go back

## Read and watch

- [About version control](https://git-scm.com/book/en/v2/Getting-Started-About-Version-Control) — Pro Git book (git-scm.com)

lessons.body:
This lesson is about **30 freeCodeCamp steps**. Work through them in order — the steps build on each other.

## What to do

- Do the first Forms and Tables workshop on freeCodeCamp
- Build a sign-up form for a club, with a label for every field

## Understand it

A form is how a page asks a question. The `<form>` element wraps the questions; each question is usually an `<input>`, and every input needs a `<label>` that says what it is for:

```html
<form action="/join" method="post">
  <label for="name">Your name</label>
  <input id="name" name="name" type="text" required>

  <label for="email">Email</label>
  <input id="email" name="email" type="email">

  <fieldset>
    <legend>Which course?</legend>
    <label><input type="radio" name="course" value="coding"> Coding</label>
    <label><input type="radio" name="course" value="media"> Media Lab</label>
  </fieldset>
  <button type="submit">Join</button>
</form>
```

The `for` on the label matches the `id` on the input. That link matters: a screen reader reads the label aloud when the field is focused, and clicking the label puts the cursor in the field — a bigger target on a phone. A placeholder is **not** a label: it disappears as soon as somebody types.

The `type` changes the keyboard a phone shows (`email` adds @, `tel` shows numbers) and gives free checking. `name` is the key the data is sent under. Radio buttons with the same `name` form a group where only one can be chosen; checkboxes allow many.

## Key words

- **label:** the visible name of a form field, linked to it with for and id
- **input type:** decides the kind of field and the phone keyboard shown
- **name:** the key a field's value is sent under when the form is submitted
- **fieldset / legend:** a group of related fields and the question they answer

## Read and watch

lessons.summary: About one in six people lives with a disability. Make pages that work with a keyboard and a screen reader, using the right elements and ARIA only where HTML has no answer.
objectives: You will check a page using only the keyboard
You will use headings in order and give images alt text
You will explain when ARIA is and is not needed
lessons.body:
This lesson is about **28 freeCodeCamp steps**. Work through them in order — the steps build on each other.

## What to do

- Do the HTML accessibility workshop on freeCodeCamp
- Use Tab to move through your page — can you reach and use everything?

## Understand it

An accessible page is one that works for people who use it differently: with a keyboard instead of a mouse, with a screen reader that speaks the page aloud, zoomed to 200%, or in bright sunlight on a cracked screen. The rules are written down as the **Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG)**, and most of them are met by good HTML alone.

Five checks you can do on any page today:

1. **Keyboard:** put the mouse away and press Tab. Can you reach every link and button, and can you see where you are?
2. **Headings:** do they go h1 → h2 → h3 in a sensible outline?
3. **Images:** does every meaningful image have alt text?
4. **Forms:** does every field have a real label?
5. **Buttons and links:** is a button a `<button>` and a link an `<a>`? A `<div>` that looks like a button cannot be reached by keyboard.

**ARIA** attributes (such as `aria-label`) add information for assistive technology, but the first rule of ARIA is: if an HTML element already does the job, use it instead. No ARIA is better than wrong ARIA.

## Key words

- **Accessibility:** making pages that work for everyone, including disabled people
- **Screen reader:** software that reads a page aloud for people who cannot see it
- **WCAG:** the international guidelines for accessible web content
- **ARIA:** extra attributes for assistive technology, used only when HTML has no answer

## Read and watch

- [Introduction to web accessibility](https://www.w3.org/WAI/fundamentals/accessibility-intro/) — W3C Web Accessibility Initiative

**GitHub Pages** turns a repository into a website for free. It takes the files in your repo and serves them at an address like `https://your-name.github.io/my-first-site/`. Anybody with the link can open it, on any phone or computer.

The steps: in your repository, open **Settings → Pages**, choose to deploy from the `main` branch and the root folder, and save. After a minute or two the address appears at the top of that page. From then on, every time you push a commit, the site updates by itself.

- **Hosting:** keeping a site on a computer that serves it to the internet

lessons.body:
This lesson is about **40 freeCodeCamp steps**. Work through them in order — the steps build on each other.

## What to do

- Work through Basic CSS on freeCodeCamp (first half)

## Understand it

Most of the CSS on any site is a handful of properties used again and again:

- `color` — the text colour; `background-color` or `background` — the colour behind it
- `border: 2px solid #ccc` — width, style and colour in one line; `border-radius` rounds the corners
- `width` and `max-width` — how wide a box is; `max-width: 60ch` keeps lines of text a comfortable length
- `padding` — space *inside* the border; `margin` — space *outside* it

Units matter. `px` is a fixed size. `%` is relative to the parent box. `rem` is relative to the page's base font size (usually 16px), so `1.5rem` is 24px — and it grows when somebody turns up their text size, which `px` sizes for text do not. `ch` is about the width of one character. A sensible default: `rem` for font sizes and spacing, `%` or `max-width` for widths.

Shorthand saves typing but can surprise you: `margin: 8px 16px` means 8px top and bottom, 16px left and right. Four values go clockwise from the top: top, right, bottom, left.

## Key words

- **padding:** space between an element's content and its border
- **margin:** space outside the border, pushing other elements away
- **rem:** a size relative to the page's base font size
- **Shorthand:** one property that sets several at once, like margin: 8px 16px

This lesson is about **40 freeCodeCamp steps**. Work through them in order — the steps build on each other.

## What to do

- Finish Basic CSS on freeCodeCamp
- **With an AI assistant —** Ask an AI assistant why a layout is not doing what you expect, paste only your own small snippet, and test each suggestion one change at a time in the browser.

## Understand it

When two rules try to style the same element, CSS needs a way to decide who wins. That is the **cascade**, and it works in this order:

1. **Importance** — rules marked `!important` beat normal ones (avoid it; it makes later changes painful).
2. **Specificity** — a more specific selector wins. An id (`#title`) beats a class (`.big`), which beats an element (`h1`). Count them like a score: ids, then classes, then elements.
3. **Order** — if two rules are equally specific, the one written *later* wins.

```css
p { color: black; }          /* specificity 0-0-1 */
.intro { color: navy; }      /* 0-1-0 — wins over p */
p.intro { color: teal; }     /* 0-1-1 — wins over .intro */
```

Some properties are **inherited**: set `font-family` or `color` on `body` and every element inside takes it unless told otherwise. Box properties such as `border` and `padding` are not inherited.

When a style is not working, open DevTools, select the element, and look at the Styles panel: rules that lost are shown crossed out, with the rule that beat them above.

## Key words

- **Cascade:** the rules CSS uses to decide which style wins
- **Specificity:** how precise a selector is; more precise beats less precise
- **Inheritance:** some styles passing from a parent element to its children
- **display:** whether an element sits on its own line (block) or inside text (inline)

## Read and watch

lessons.body:
This lesson is about **40 freeCodeCamp steps**. Work through them in order — the steps build on each other.

## What to do

- Do the box model lessons on freeCodeCamp
- In the developer tools, hover over an element and read its box model diagram

## Understand it

Every element on a page is a rectangle made of four layers, from the inside out:

1. **Content** — the text or image
2. **Padding** — space around the content, inside the border; it takes the background colour
3. **Border** — the line around the padding
4. **Margin** — space outside the border that keeps other elements away; always transparent

By default, `width` sets only the *content* width, so a box with `width: 300px; padding: 20px; border: 2px solid` actually takes 344px. That surprises everybody. Most developers put this at the top of every stylesheet:

```css
*, *::before, *::after { box-sizing: border-box; }
```

Now `width: 300px` means the whole box, padding and border included, is 300px.

Two more facts that save hours: vertical margins between two blocks **collapse** (a 20px bottom margin above a 30px top margin gives 30px, not 50px); and inline elements such as `<a>` or `<span>` ignore width, height and top/bottom margin until you set `display: inline-block` or `block`.

## Key words

- **Box model:** content, padding, border and margin — the layers of every element
- **box-sizing: border-box:** makes width include padding and border
- **Margin collapse:** two vertical margins meeting become the larger one, not the sum

lessons.body:
This lesson is about **49 freeCodeCamp steps**. Work through them in order — the steps build on each other.

## What to do

- Do the Colors workshop on freeCodeCamp
- Pick a palette of four colours for your site and check text contrast with a contrast checker

## Understand it

Screens mix red, green and blue light. CSS lets you write a colour three main ways:

- **Hex:** `#16233f` — two digits each for red, green, blue, from 00 to ff
- **rgb():** `rgb(22 35 63)` — the same three amounts, 0 to 255; add `/ 50%` for transparency
- **hsl():** `hsl(220 48% 17%)` — hue (the colour, 0–360 round a wheel), saturation (how strong), lightness (how light). HSL is the easiest to adjust by hand: keep the hue, change the lightness, and you have a matching lighter shade.

Colour must also be **readable**. Contrast is measured as a ratio between text and background, from 1:1 (same colour) to 21:1 (black on white). WCAG asks for at least **4.5:1** for normal text and 3:1 for large text. Light grey on white often fails — and in Lagos sunlight on a phone at half brightness, it fails worse.

Never use colour as the *only* signal. About 1 in 12 men cannot easily tell red from green, so an error message should say "Error" or show an icon, not just turn red.

## Key words

- **Hex colour:** a colour written as # and six digits for red, green and blue
- **HSL:** hue, saturation and lightness — an easy way to make shades
- **Contrast ratio:** how different text and background are; 4.5:1 is the minimum for body text

## Read and watch

lessons.body:
This lesson is about **45 freeCodeCamp steps**. Work through them in order — the steps build on each other.

## What to do

- Do the Responsive Design lessons on freeCodeCamp
- Make your page work at 360px wide, then add a min-width media query for larger screens
- **With an AI assistant —** Ask an AI assistant why a layout is not doing what you expect, paste only your own small snippet, and test each suggestion one change at a time in the browser.

## Understand it

A **responsive** page rearranges itself to fit the screen it is on. **Mobile first** means you write the CSS for the smallest screen first — usually one column, full width — and then add rules for bigger screens with **media queries**:

```css
.gallery { display: grid; gap: 12px; }

@media (min-width: 640px) {
  .gallery { grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr; }
}
@media (min-width: 1024px) {
  .gallery { grid-template-columns: repeat(4, 1fr); }
}
```

Why small first? The phone layout is the simplest, so starting there keeps the CSS short; and most visitors in Nigeria browse on a phone, often on mobile data, so the phone is the main event, not an afterthought.

Good habits: never set a fixed width wider than about 320px; use `max-width: 100%` on images so they shrink; keep tap targets at least 44px tall; and test by dragging the DevTools device toolbar down to 360px wide. If the page scrolls sideways, something is too wide — find it before your users do.

## Key words

- **Responsive design:** pages that adapt their layout to the screen size
- **Media query:** CSS that applies only when a condition is true, like min-width: 640px
- **Mobile first:** writing the phone layout first and adding to it for larger screens
- **Breakpoint:** a width at which the layout changes

lessons.body:
This lesson is about **45 freeCodeCamp steps**. Work through them in order — the steps build on each other.

## What to do

- Do the Flexbox workshop on freeCodeCamp
- Lay out your nav links in a row with even spacing

## Understand it

**Flexbox** lays items out in one direction — a row or a column — and shares out the space. You switch it on for a **container**, and its direct children become **flex items**:

```css
nav ul {
  display: flex;
  gap: 16px;                 /* space between items */
  justify-content: space-between;  /* along the main direction */
  align-items: center;       /* across it */
  flex-wrap: wrap;           /* allow a new line when there is no room */
}
```

Two words unlock everything: the **main axis** is the direction items flow (`flex-direction: row` is left to right); the **cross axis** runs the other way. `justify-content` places items along the main axis (`flex-start`, `center`, `space-between`); `align-items` places them on the cross axis.

On a child, `flex: 1` means "take an equal share of the spare room" — a quick way to make three cards the same width. Flexbox is the tool for nav bars, button rows, a picture beside some text, and centring something in a box — for years the hardest trick in CSS, now two lines.

## Key words

- **Flex container:** the parent with display: flex
- **Main axis:** the direction flex items flow in
- **justify-content:** places items along the main axis
- **align-items:** places items across the main axis

## What to do

- Do the Typography workshop on freeCodeCamp
- Set your body text to 1rem with a line-height of about 1.5

## Understand it

Typography is most of a page's design, because most of a page is text. Four decisions do most of the work:

1. **Font family.** Pick one family for body text and at most one more for headings. Always give fallbacks: `font-family: "Inter", system-ui, sans-serif;`. System fonts load instantly and cost no data.
2. **Size.** Body text at `1rem` (16px) is the minimum on a phone; smaller strains eyes. Headings step up in a clear scale, such as 1.25, 1.5, 2, 2.5rem.
3. **Line height.** About `1.5` for body text gives the eye room to find the next line; headings can be tighter, around 1.2.
4. **Line length.** 45 to 75 characters per line is comfortable to read. `max-width: 65ch` on a text column does it.

Also: left-align body text (justified text makes uneven gaps), use `font-weight` 600–700 for emphasis rather than capitals, and do not let a light grey font fail contrast. Readable beats pretty every time — a beautiful page nobody can read is a broken page.

## Key words

- **Font stack:** a list of fonts to try in order, ending in a generic family
- **line-height:** the height of each line of text, as a multiple of the font size
- **Measure:** the length of a line of text; 45–75 characters is comfortable

lessons.body:
This lesson is about **50 freeCodeCamp steps**. Work through them in order — the steps build on each other.

## What to do

- Do the positioning lessons on freeCodeCamp
- Make your page header stick to the top as you scroll
- **With an AI assistant —** ask it to *explain* a tag you are unsure of, then check it on MDN (developer.mozilla.org). Type the code yourself — copying code you cannot explain is not learning.

## Understand it

Normally elements flow down the page one after another. The `position` property takes an element out of that flow in four ways:

- `relative` — the element stays in the flow, but `top`/`left` nudge it from where it would have been. Its main use is to become the reference point for an absolute child.
- `absolute` — removed from the flow and placed relative to the nearest **positioned** ancestor. Use it for a badge on a card's corner.
- `fixed` — placed relative to the screen; it stays put when you scroll. A chat button in the corner.
- `sticky` — scrolls normally until it reaches a point (such as `top: 0`), then sticks. Perfect for a header or table heading.

```css
.card { position: relative; }
.card .badge { position: absolute; top: 8px; right: 8px; }
header { position: sticky; top: 0; z-index: 10; background: white; }
```

`z-index` decides which overlapping element is on top — but only among positioned elements, and only within the same **stacking context**. If a z-index of 9999 is not working, the problem is the context, not the number.

## Key words

- **position:** how an element is placed: static, relative, absolute, fixed or sticky
- **Normal flow:** how elements lay out when nothing changes it
- **z-index:** which positioned element is drawn on top
- **Stacking context:** a group of elements layered together; z-index works within it

lessons.body:
This lesson is about **45 freeCodeCamp steps**. Work through them in order — the steps build on each other.

## What to do

- Do the pseudo-classes and attribute selectors lessons on freeCodeCamp

## Understand it

A **pseudo-class** styles an element in a particular *state*. It is written with one colon:

- `a:hover` — when the mouse is over a link
- `button:focus-visible` — when the keyboard is on it
- `input:disabled`, `input:checked`
- `li:first-child`, `li:nth-child(odd)` — by position, for striped lists

A **pseudo-element** styles a *part* of an element, or adds decoration, with two colons:

- `p::first-line`, `p::first-letter`
- `.note::before { content: "Note: "; font-weight: 700; }` — adds content before

**Attribute selectors** pick elements by their attributes:

```css
a[href^="https"] { }     /* href starts with https */
a[href$=".pdf"]::after { content: " (PDF)"; }  /* ends with .pdf */
input[type="email"] { }
```

These let you style without adding classes everywhere. One caution: text added with `::before` is decoration — some screen readers skip it — so never put essential information there.

## Key words

- **Pseudo-class:** a state of an element, like :hover or :focus
- **Pseudo-element:** a part of an element, like ::before or ::first-line
- **Attribute selector:** selects elements by an attribute, like [type="email"]

## Understand it

**Custom properties** (CSS variables) let you name a value once and use it everywhere:

```css
:root {
  --brand: #16233f;
  --accent: #f5b026;
  --space: 16px;
}
.button {
  background: var(--brand);
  padding: calc(var(--space) / 2) var(--space);
}
.button:hover { background: var(--accent); }
```

`:root` is the top of the page, so variables set there are available everywhere. Names start with two dashes. `var(--name)` reads one, and `var(--name, red)` gives a fallback if it is missing.

Unlike variables in some other tools, these are **live**: change one and everything using it updates at once — even from JavaScript, or inside a media query. That makes dark mode a few lines: redefine the colours for `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` and the whole site follows.

A site with five colour variables and four spacing variables stays consistent by itself. A site with forty slightly different hand-typed greys does not — and that inconsistency is what makes a page look amateur.

## Key words

- **Custom property:** a named value starting with -- that CSS can reuse
- **var():** reads a custom property's value
- **:root:** the top element of the page, where global variables live
- **calc():** does arithmetic with CSS values

lessons.body:
This lesson is about **40 freeCodeCamp steps**. Work through them in order — the steps build on each other.

## What to do

- Do the first CSS Grid workshop on freeCodeCamp

## Understand it

Flexbox works in one direction; **CSS Grid** works in two — rows *and* columns at once. You define the tracks on the container and items fall into the cells:

```css
.page {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: 200px 1fr;   /* a sidebar and the rest */
  grid-template-rows: auto 1fr auto;  /* header, content, footer */
  gap: 16px;
}
.page header { grid-column: 1 / -1; }  /* span every column */
```

The `fr` unit means "a fraction of the free space": `1fr 2fr` gives the second column twice the room of the first. `repeat(3, 1fr)` is three equal columns. Lines between tracks are numbered from 1, and `-1` is the last line, so `grid-column: 1 / -1` stretches an item across the whole width.

Turn on the **Grid** badge in DevTools (next to the element in the Elements panel) and it draws the lines and their numbers over the page — the fastest way to understand why something landed where it did.

## Key words

- **Grid container:** the parent with display: grid
- **Track:** one row or one column of a grid
- **fr:** a fraction of the free space in a grid
- **Grid line:** the numbered lines between tracks, used to place items

This lesson is about **45 freeCodeCamp steps**. Work through them in order — the steps build on each other.

## What to do

- Do the CSS accessibility and design lessons on freeCodeCamp
- Review your site: is it obvious what matters most on each page?
- **With an AI assistant —** Ask an AI assistant why a layout is not doing what you expect, paste only your own small snippet, and test each suggestion one change at a time in the browser.

## Understand it

Design is not decoration; it is making the important thing obvious. Four principles do most of it:

- **Hierarchy** — the most important thing is the biggest, boldest or highest. A visitor should know in three seconds what a page is for.
- **Spacing** — related things sit close; unrelated things are separated. More space between sections than inside them groups content without any lines.
- **Alignment** — line things up on a few edges. A page where every item starts at a slightly different point looks careless even if nobody can say why.
- **Contrast** — not only colour: big against small, bold against light, filled against empty.

And three CSS habits that keep a design usable:

```css
:focus-visible { outline: 3px solid var(--accent); outline-offset: 2px; }
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  * { animation: none; transition: none; }
}
html { font-size: 100%; }   /* respect the reader's own text size */
```

Some people get dizzy or sick from movement on screen, and their phone's "reduce motion" setting tells you so — honour it. Never remove the focus outline without a better one.

## Key words

- **Visual hierarchy:** arranging a page so the most important thing is seen first
- **Whitespace:** empty space that groups and separates content
- **prefers-reduced-motion:** a media query for people who asked their device for less movement

lessons.body:
This lesson is about **45 freeCodeCamp steps**. Work through them in order — the steps build on each other.

## What to do

- Finish the CSS Animation workshops on freeCodeCamp

## Understand it

The `animation` shorthand packs eight settings into one line. Written out:

```css
.loader {
  animation-name: spin;
  animation-duration: 1s;
  animation-timing-function: linear;
  animation-delay: 200ms;
  animation-iteration-count: infinite;   /* or a number */
  animation-direction: alternate;        /* forwards then backwards */
  animation-fill-mode: forwards;         /* keep the last frame */
  animation-play-state: running;
}
```

**Delays** let you stagger: give a list of cards delays of 0, 80 and 160ms and they arrive one after another. **Fill mode** decides what the element looks like before the animation starts and after it ends — `forwards` keeps the final frame instead of snapping back.

Transforms combine in one property, applied right to left: `transform: translateX(20px) rotate(10deg) scale(1.1);`. Order matters — rotating then moving is not the same as moving then rotating.

`cubic-bezier()` lets you design your own easing curve; DevTools has a visual editor for it. Try a little overshoot, such as `cubic-bezier(0.34, 1.56, 0.64, 1)`, for a playful bounce — then ask whether the page needs one.

## Key words

- **animation-delay:** how long to wait before an animation starts
- **animation-fill-mode:** what an element looks like before and after its animation
- **cubic-bezier:** a custom easing curve

1. **The brief.** Who is the site for, and what must they be able to do? "A site for Mama Nkechi's catering so customers can see the menu, prices and how to order on WhatsApp" is a brief. "A food website" is not.

lessons.body:
This lesson is about **50 freeCodeCamp steps**. Work through them in order — the steps build on each other.

## What to do

- Do the first part of the JavaScript fundamentals (variables and strings) on freeCodeCamp
- **With an AI assistant —** Use an AI assistant as a tutor: ask it to explain an error message line by line, then fix the bug yourself. Ask "why" until you could explain it to a classmate.

## Understand it

HTML says what things are, CSS how they look, and **JavaScript** what they *do*. It is a real programming language: it stores values, makes decisions and repeats work.

A **variable** is a named box for a value:

```js
const name = "Ada";       // const: will not be reassigned
let score = 0;            // let: can change
score = score + 10;
console.log(name, score); // prints: Ada 10
```

Use `const` by default and `let` only when the value must change. (You will see `var` in old code; avoid it.) Names are camelCase: `totalScore`, not `total score`.

Text is a **string**, in quotes. Join strings with **template literals** — backticks with `${}` slots:

```js
const centre = "Egbeda";
const greeting = `Welcome, ${name}, to ${centre}!`;
greeting.length;          // how many characters
greeting.toUpperCase();
greeting.includes("Egbeda");  // true
```

The **console** (DevTools → Console) runs JavaScript immediately. Use it constantly: type a line, see what it does. That is how professionals try ideas.

## Key words

## What to do

## Understand it

Numbers work as you would expect — `+ - * /` — plus `%`, the **remainder**: `17 % 5` is 2, handy for "is this even?" (`n % 2 === 0`). Be careful: `"5" + 3` is `"53"`, because `+` joins strings. Turn text into a number first with `Number("5")`.

A **boolean** is `true` or `false`, usually the answer to a comparison:

```js
age >= 13          // greater than or equal
name === "Ada"     // strictly equal: same value AND same type
score !== 0        // not equal
```

Always use `===`, not `==`. The double version converts types first, so `0 == ""` is true — a source of strange bugs.

**Conditions** make code choose:

```js
if (score >= 70) {
  message = "Distinction";
} else if (score >= 50) {
  message = "Pass";
} else {
  message = "Try again";
}
```

Combine tests with `&&` (and), `||` (or) and `!` (not): `if (age >= 10 && age <= 17)`. Checks run top to bottom and stop at the first that is true, so put the narrowest condition first.

- **Boolean:** a value that is either true or false
- **===:** strict equality: same value and same type

## Understand it

A **function** is a named recipe: write the steps once, then use them as often as you like.

```js
function grade(score) {
  if (score >= 70) return "Distinction";
  if (score >= 50) return "Pass";
  return "Try again";

grade(41);   // "Try again"
```

`score` is a **parameter** — a name for the value passed in. `82` is the **argument** — the actual value. `return` sends a result back and ends the function immediately; a function without it returns `undefined`.

The same idea as an **arrow function**, which you will see everywhere in modern code:

```js
const double = (n) => n * 2;
```

Good functions do **one job** and are named with a verb that says what: `calculateTotal`, `showError`, `isValidEmail`. If you cannot name a function in a few words, it is doing too much — split it.

Variables made inside a function exist only inside it. That is called **scope**, and it is a feature: it stops one part of a program accidentally changing another.

- **Function:** a named, reusable block of code
- **Parameter / argument:** the name inside the function / the value you pass in

- Do the Arrays lessons on freeCodeCamp

## Understand it

An **array** is an ordered list of values in square brackets:

```js
const courses = ["Coding", "Media Lab", "Chess"];
courses[0];          // "Coding" — counting starts at 0
courses.length;      // 3
courses[courses.length - 1];  // the last item
```

The everyday methods:

```js
courses.push("Piano");        // add to the end
courses.pop();                // remove from the end
courses.unshift("Robotics");  // add to the start
courses.includes("Chess");    // true
courses.indexOf("Media Lab"); // its position, or -1 if missing
courses.slice(0, 2);          // a copy of the first two
courses.join(", ");           // "Robotics, Coding, Media Lab, Chess"
```

Off-by-one errors are the classic array bug: an array of 3 items has positions 0, 1 and 2, so `courses[3]` is `undefined`. When a loop or index misbehaves, check the first and last positions first.

`const` stops you replacing the array with a different one, but you can still change what is *inside* it. That surprises everybody once.

## Key words

- **Array:** an ordered list of values
- **Index:** an item's position, counted from 0
- **push / pop:** add to / remove from the end of an array

## Understand it

An array is good for a list of similar things. An **object** groups different facts about *one* thing under names:

```js
const learner = {
  name: "Tobi",
  age: 13,
  centre: "Egbeda",
  courses: ["Coding", "Chess"],
};

learner.email = "t@example.org";  // add a property
```

```js
const counter = { count: 0, add() { this.count++; } };
```

Most real data is an **array of objects**: a list of learners, a list of products, a list of messages. When you fetch data from a server later, it will arrive in exactly this shape — so get comfortable reading `learners[2].courses[0]` from left to right.

## Key words

## What to do

- Do the JavaScript fundamentals review and higher-order functions lessons on freeCodeCamp

## Understand it

In JavaScript a function is a value: you can pass it to another function. Functions that take functions are **higher-order functions**, and three of them replace most loops over arrays:

```js
const scores = [45, 82, 67, 90, 38];

scores.map(s => s + 5);          // [50, 87, 72, 95, 43]   — change every item
scores.filter(s => s >= 50);     // [82, 67, 90]           — keep some items
scores.reduce((sum, s) => sum + s, 0);   // 322         — combine into one value
```

- **map** makes a new array of the same length, each item transformed.
- **filter** makes a new array with only the items that pass a test.
- **reduce** walks the array carrying a running result — a total, a maximum, a count.

They chain: `learners.filter(l => l.centre === "Egbeda").map(l => l.name)` gives the names of Egbeda's learners. None of them change the original array; they return a new one, which makes bugs less likely.

Other useful ones: `find` (the first match), `some` and `every` (true or false), `sort` (careful — it *does* change the original, and sorts numbers as text unless you give it `(a, b) => a - b`).

## Key words

- **Higher-order function:** a function that takes or returns another function
- **map:** makes a new array with every item transformed
- **filter:** makes a new array with only the items that pass a test
- **reduce:** combines an array into a single value

## Understand it

When a browser reads your HTML it builds the **DOM** (Document Object Model): a tree of objects, one for every element. JavaScript can find any branch of that tree and change it, and the page updates instantly.

```js
const title = document.querySelector("h1");           // the first h1
const cards = document.querySelectorAll(".card");     // every .card

title.textContent = "Welcome back, Ada";
title.classList.add("is-highlighted");
cards.forEach(card => card.classList.toggle("is-open"));

const item = document.createElement("li");
item.textContent = "New task";
document.querySelector("#tasks").append(item);
```

`querySelector` uses the same selectors as CSS, so everything you learnt there works here. Change **classes** rather than writing styles directly from JavaScript: the CSS decides how `.is-highlighted` looks, the JavaScript only decides *when*. That keeps the two jobs apart.

Use `textContent` to put text on the page. `innerHTML` reads text as HTML, so if any of it came from a user it can run their code on your page — a security hole called cross-site scripting.

## Key words

- **DOM:** the tree of objects the browser builds from your HTML
- **querySelector:** finds the first element matching a CSS selector
- **classList:** adds, removes or toggles an element's classes
- **textContent:** an element's text, set safely

## What to do

- Do the Debugging lessons on freeCodeCamp
- Set a breakpoint in your counter and step through it
- **With an AI assistant —** use it only to explain, suggest or check — never to produce your work for you. Write down what you asked, what it said, and how you checked it.

## Understand it

Every programmer writes bugs every day. The skill is finding them calmly. A method that works:

1. **Read the error message — all of it.** `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'name') at app.js:14` tells you the file, the line, and that something you expected to be an object was `undefined`.
2. **Reproduce it.** Find the exact steps that cause it every time.
3. **Narrow it down.** Put `console.log()` before the failing line to see what each value really is. The bug is almost always where your belief about a value differs from the truth.
4. **Use a breakpoint.** In DevTools → Sources, click a line number. The code pauses there and you can see every variable and step forward line by line.
5. **Change one thing at a time,** then test. Changing five things at once hides which one mattered.

The three error types you will meet most: `ReferenceError` (a name that does not exist — often a typo), `TypeError` (using a value the wrong way, such as calling something that is not a function), and `SyntaxError` (code the browser cannot read at all — a missing bracket or quote).

Explaining the problem out loud to somebody — or to a rubber duck — solves a surprising number of bugs before they say a word.

## Key words

- **Bug:** a mistake that makes code behave wrongly
- **Stack trace:** the list of where an error happened, with file and line
- **Breakpoint:** a line where DevTools pauses your code so you can inspect it
- **console.log:** prints a value so you can see what it really is

## What to do

## Understand it

A **regular expression** (regex) is a pattern for text. It lets you ask "does this look like a phone number?" or "find every word that starts with a capital".

```js
const ngPhone = /^0[789][01]\d{8}$/;
ngPhone.test("08031234567");   // true
ngPhone.test("0803123");       // false
```

Reading that pattern piece by piece: `^` start of the text; `0` the digit zero; `[789]` one of 7, 8 or 9; `[01]` a 0 or 1; `\d{8}` exactly eight digits; `$` end of the text.

The building blocks:

- `.` any character; `\d` a digit; `\w` a letter, digit or _; `\s` a space
- `[abc]` one of these; `[^abc]` anything but these
- `*` zero or more; `+` one or more; `?` optional; `{2,4}` between two and four
- `( )` a group; `|` or
- flags: `i` ignore case, `g` find all matches

```js
"Lagos, Ibadan, Abeokuta".match(/\b[A-Z]\w+/g);  // ["Lagos", "Ibadan", "Abeokuta"]
"  too   many   spaces ".replace(/\s+/g, " ").trim();
```

Test patterns on a site like regex101 before trusting them, and keep them simple: a regex nobody can read is a bug waiting to happen.

## Key words

- **Regular expression:** a pattern that describes text
- **^ and $:** the start and end of the text
- **Quantifier:** how many times something repeats: *, +, ?, {n}
- **Flag:** an option on a regex, like g (global) or i (ignore case)

## What to do

- Finish the Form Validation workshops on freeCodeCamp

## Understand it

Live feedback — checking a field as somebody types or when they leave it — saves them a frustrating trip back from the submit button. Check on `blur` (leaving the field) rather than on every keystroke, so people are not told they are wrong before they have finished typing.

The **Constraint Validation API** lets JavaScript use the browser's own checking and add your own rules:

```js
const pass = form.elements.password;
const confirm = form.elements.confirm;

confirm.addEventListener("input", () => {
  confirm.setCustomValidity(
    confirm.value === pass.value ? "" : "The two passwords do not match."
  );
});
if (!form.checkValidity()) form.reportValidity();
```

An empty string from `setCustomValidity` means "valid".

And the most important rule of all: **the server must check again.** Anything in the browser can be switched off — anybody can open DevTools, delete `required`, or send data straight to your server without using your page at all. Browser validation is a convenience for honest users. Server validation is the protection. You will build that in the back-end weeks.

## Key words

- **blur:** the event when a field loses focus
- **setCustomValidity:** sets your own error message on a field
- **Server-side validation:** checking data on the server, where users cannot switch it off

lessons.body:
This lesson is about **30 freeCodeCamp steps**. Work through them in order — the steps build on each other.

## What to do

- Do the Dates lessons on freeCodeCamp

## Understand it

JavaScript's `Date` object holds a moment in time:

```js
const now = new Date();
now.getFullYear();      // 2026
now.getMonth();         // 0–11 — January is 0!
now.getDay();           // 0–6 — Sunday is 0

const start = new Date("2026-10-03T10:00:00");
const ms = now - start;                 // the difference in milliseconds
const days = Math.floor(ms / 86400000); // 1000 * 60 * 60 * 24
```

Internally a date is a number: the milliseconds since 1 January 1970. That is why subtracting two dates gives a duration.

To **show** a date, let the browser format it for the reader's language and region instead of building the string yourself:

```js
now.toLocaleDateString("en-GB", { weekday: "long", day: "numeric", month: "long" });
// "Saturday 3 October"
now.toLocaleTimeString("en-GB", { hour: "2-digit", minute: "2-digit" });
```

Time zones are the classic trap. A server in Europe and a learner in Lagos (UTC+1) can disagree about what "today" is around midnight. Store dates in a standard form — ISO strings like `2026-10-03T09:00:00Z` — and convert only when showing them.

## Key words

- **Date:** JavaScript's object for a moment in time
- **Timestamp:** a date stored as milliseconds since 1 January 1970
- **ISO 8601:** the standard date format, like 2026-10-03T09:00:00Z
- **Time zone:** a region's offset from UTC; Lagos is UTC+1

lessons.body:

## Understand it

Arrays and objects cover most needs; two more structures fill the gaps.

A **Set** is a collection where every value appears once:

```js
const tags = new Set(["html", "css", "html"]);
tags.size;              // 2 — the duplicate is ignored
tags.add("js");
tags.has("css");        // true, and fast even with thousands of items
const unique = [...new Set(list)];   // remove duplicates from an array
```

A **Map** stores values by **key**, like an object, but any value can be a key and it remembers the order things were added:

```js
const attendance = new Map();
attendance.set("Tobi", 11);
attendance.set("Kemi", 12);
attendance.get("Kemi");        // 12
attendance.has("Ada");         // false
for (const [name, days] of attendance) console.log(name, days);
```

When to use which: an **array** for an ordered list you go through; a **Set** for "is this in the group?" and removing duplicates; a **Map** for looking things up by a key, especially when keys are added and removed while the program runs; a plain **object** for a fixed record with known property names.

## Key words

- **Set:** a collection with no repeated values
- **Map:** a collection of key → value pairs
- **Key:** the name you look a value up by

lessons.body:
This lesson is about **65 freeCodeCamp steps**. Work through them in order — the steps build on each other.

## What to do

- Do the localStorage and CRUD workshop on freeCodeCamp
- Build a to-do list that keeps its items after a refresh

## Understand it

Variables vanish when the page reloads. **localStorage** keeps data in the browser, on that device, until it is deleted:

```js
localStorage.setItem("name", "Ada");
localStorage.getItem("name");      // "Ada"
localStorage.removeItem("name");
```

It stores only **strings**, so turn arrays and objects into text with JSON:

```js
function save(tasks) { localStorage.setItem("tasks", JSON.stringify(tasks)); }
function load() { return JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem("tasks")) || []; }
```

Almost every app does four things to its data, known as **CRUD**:

- **Create** — add a task: `tasks.push({ id: Date.now(), text, done: false })`
- **Read** — show them: loop and build the list
- **Update** — tick one off: find it by `id` and change `done`
- **Delete** — `tasks = tasks.filter(t => t.id !== id)`

After every change: save, then redraw the list from the data. Keeping one source of truth (the array) and drawing the page from it is the idea every front-end framework is built on.

localStorage is per browser and per device, and anyone using that device can read it — never store passwords or private information in it.

## Key words

- **localStorage:** browser storage that survives a page reload
- **JSON:** a text format for data; JSON.stringify and JSON.parse convert to and from it
- **CRUD:** create, read, update, delete — what apps do to data
- **Single source of truth:** keeping data in one place and drawing the page from it

lessons.body:
This lesson is about **46 freeCodeCamp steps**. Work through them in order — the steps build on each other.

## What to do

- Do the Functional Programming lessons on freeCodeCamp
- **With an AI assistant —** Use an AI assistant as a tutor: ask it to explain an error message line by line, then fix the bug yourself. Ask "why" until you could explain it to a classmate.

## Understand it

**Functional programming** is a style built on small functions that are easy to trust. Two ideas carry most of it.

A **pure function** gives the same output for the same input and changes nothing outside itself:

```js
// pure: same input, same output, no side effects
const withTax = (price) => price * 1.075;

// impure: changes something outside, so calling it twice is different
let total = 0;
function addToTotal(price) { total += price; }
```

**Immutability** means not changing data in place but making a new copy with the change:

```js
const learner = { name: "Kemi", level: 2 };
const promoted = { ...learner, level: 3 };          // learner is untouched
const more = [...courses, "Robotics"];               // a new array
```

Why bother? Pure functions can be tested on their own, reused anywhere, and never surprise you by breaking something elsewhere. Most bugs in larger programs come from one part changing data another part was relying on.

You already use the style: `map`, `filter` and `reduce` are functional tools. Programs combine small pure functions and keep the impure parts — saving, fetching, drawing the page — together at the edges.

## Key words

- **Pure function:** same input always gives the same output, with no side effects
- **Side effect:** a change outside a function, such as editing a global or the page
- **Immutability:** making changed copies instead of editing data in place

objectives: You will write a base case and a recursive case

lessons.body:
This lesson is about **35 freeCodeCamp steps**. Work through them in order — the steps build on each other.

## What to do

- Do the Recursion lessons on freeCodeCamp

## Understand it

A **recursive** function solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller piece of the same problem. Every recursive function needs two parts:

1. a **base case** — a version so small it can be answered directly, which stops the recursion;
2. a **recursive case** — break the problem down and call yourself on the smaller part.

```js
function countdown(n) {
  if (n === 0) { console.log("Lift off!"); return; }   // base case
  console.log(n);
  countdown(n - 1);                                     // smaller problem
}

function sum(list) {
  if (list.length === 0) return 0;
  return list[0] + sum(list.slice(1));
}
```

Recursion is the natural tool for **nested** data — folders inside folders, comments with replies to replies, a family tree — where you do not know how deep it goes:

```js
function countFiles(folder) {
  return folder.files.length + folder.folders.reduce((n, f) => n + countFiles(f), 0);
}
```

Forget the base case and the function calls itself forever until the browser stops it with "Maximum call stack size exceeded". When writing one, write the base case first.

## Key words

- **Recursion:** a function that calls itself on a smaller version of the problem
- **Base case:** the simplest case, answered directly, that stops recursion
- **Call stack:** the list of functions currently running, waiting for answers

## Read and watch

lessons.body:
## What to do

- Read the MDN overview of HTTP
- Open the Network tab in the developer tools and watch a page load

## Understand it

Until now you have been the *client*. Now you build the *server* — so you need to know the conversation exactly.

An **HTTP request** has:

- a **method** — `GET` (read), `POST` (create), `PUT`/`PATCH` (update), `DELETE`
- a **path** — `/api/tasks/12`
- **headers** — extra information, such as `Content-Type: application/json`
- sometimes a **body** — the data being sent

The **response** has a **status code**, headers and a body:

- `200 OK`, `201 Created`, `204 No Content`
- `400 Bad Request` (your data was wrong), `401` (sign in), `403` (not allowed), `404 Not Found`
- `500 Internal Server Error` (the server broke)

The first digit tells you whose problem it is: 2 — success; 4 — the client asked wrongly; 5 — the server failed.

The body is usually **JSON** — text that looks like JavaScript objects, with double quotes on every key:

```json
{ "id": 12, "title": "Finish the capstone", "done": false }
```

Open DevTools → **Network**, reload any page, and click a request. You can see every one of these parts for real.

## Key words

lessons.body:
## What to do

- Add express.json() and a logging middleware
- Serve your JavaScript project's files with express.static

## Understand it

**Middleware** is a function that runs on a request *before* your route handler — like a security check at a gate. It can read or change the request, end it early, or pass it on with `next()`:

```js
app.use(express.json());             // read JSON bodies into req.body

app.use((req, res, next) => {        // log every request
  console.log(new Date().toISOString(), req.method, req.url);
  next();                             // hand over to the next middleware or route
});

app.use(express.static("public"));   // serve files in /public as they are
```

Order matters: middleware runs in the order you write `app.use`. Put `express.json()` before routes that need `req.body`, or `req.body` will be undefined — a very common bug.

`express.static("public")` turns your server into a web host too: put your front end (HTML, CSS, JS) in a `public` folder, and `http://localhost:3000/` serves `public/index.html`. Now one server delivers both the page and the API it talks to, from the same address — which also avoids browser cross-origin rules for now.

Forgetting to call `next()` (or to send a response) leaves the request hanging: the browser waits and eventually times out.

## Key words

- **Middleware:** a function that runs on requests before the route handler
- **next():** passes the request on to the next middleware or route
- **express.static:** serves files from a folder as they are
- **express.json:** middleware that reads a JSON request body into req.body

## What to do

- Test every route, including with bad input
- Return 400 for invalid data and 404 for missing items

## Understand it

An API is only as good as its worst input. Test every route with good data **and** bad:

- POST with no title, an empty title, a title of 5,000 characters, a number instead of text
- GET, PATCH and DELETE with an id that does not exist
- A body that is not valid JSON at all

You can test from the browser console with `fetch`, or use a tool like the Thunder Client extension in VS Code, or `curl` in a terminal:

```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/tasks -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"title":""}'
```

Each should get the right status and a clear message: **400** for invalid data (`{ "error": "title_required" }`), **404** for a missing item. Never let bad input reach a crash.

Catch everything else with an **error-handling middleware** — the one with four arguments — placed after all routes:

```js
app.use((err, req, res, next) => {
  console.error(err);
  res.status(500).json({ error: "server_error" });
});
```

Log the full error on the server for yourself, but send the user only a short, safe message: an error's details can reveal how your system works to somebody looking for a way in.

## Key words

- **Input validation:** checking request data before using it
- **400 Bad Request:** the status for data the server cannot accept
- **Error-handling middleware:** an Express function with (err, req, res, next) that catches failures
- **curl:** a command-line tool for sending HTTP requests

## What to do

- Create a free MongoDB Atlas cluster
- Insert and find a few documents in the Atlas interface
- **With an AI assistant —** ask it to describe what a request or query does, then test it with sample data first. AI can invent functions that do not exist — check the official docs.

## Understand it

Data kept in a JavaScript array lives in the server's memory, so it disappears whenever the server restarts — and hosts restart servers all the time. A **database** keeps data on disk, safely, and lets many users read and write at once.

There are two big families:

- **Relational** (SQL) databases — MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQLite — store data in tables with fixed columns, like a strict spreadsheet, and link tables together.
- **Document** databases — such as **MongoDB** — store **documents** that look like JSON objects, grouped into **collections**.

```json
{ "_id": "6720f1…", "title": "Finish the capstone", "done": false, "tags": ["school"], "createdAt": "2026-10-30T09:00:00Z" }
```

MongoDB suits this course because its documents are the same shape as the JavaScript objects you already use. Each document gets a unique `_id` automatically.

Model sensibly: one collection per kind of thing (tasks, users), field names that say what they hold, and the same type every time (a date always a date, never sometimes a string). **MongoDB Atlas** offers a free cloud cluster — and requires you to choose who can connect, so allow only your own IP or your host.

## Key words

- **Database:** software that stores data permanently and safely
- **Document:** one record in MongoDB, shaped like a JSON object
- **Collection:** a group of documents of the same kind
- **SQL vs NoSQL:** table-based databases vs document and other databases

lessons.body:
## What to do

- Follow the Mongoose quick start
- Make a Task model with a required title

## Understand it

**Mongoose** is a Node library that sits between your code and MongoDB. Its main job is the **schema** — a description of what each document must look like, checked every time you save:

```js
const mongoose = require("mongoose");

const taskSchema = new mongoose.Schema({
  title: { type: String, required: true, trim: true, maxlength: 200 },
  done:  { type: Boolean, default: false },
}, { timestamps: true });   // adds createdAt and updatedAt

const Task = mongoose.model("Task", taskSchema);
```

The **model** is how you work with the collection:

```js
const t = await Task.create({ title: "Revise CSS grid" });  // create
const all = await Task.find({ done: false }).sort({ createdAt: -1 });  // read
const one = await Task.findById(id);
await Task.findByIdAndUpdate(id, { done: true }, { new: true });  // update
await Task.findByIdAndDelete(id);                                 // delete
```

Every call is asynchronous, so `await` it inside an `async` function. If a document breaks the schema — no title, a title of 500 characters — Mongoose refuses to save it and throws a **ValidationError**, which you can turn into a 400 response. The database is now guarding your data, not just storing it.

## Key words

- **Mongoose:** a Node library for working with MongoDB using schemas
- **Schema:** the rules for the shape of a document
- **Model:** the object you use to create, find, update and delete documents
- **ValidationError:** Mongoose's error when a document breaks the schema

lessons.summary: Keep secrets out of your code, check every input on the server, and never store passwords as plain text.
objectives: You will keep secrets in environment variables

lessons.body:
## What to do

- Move your database connection string into a .env file and add .env to .gitignore
- Add server-side validation to your create route
- **With an AI assistant —** ask it to explain a git command before you run it. Never paste passwords, tokens or keys into any AI tool or into a public repository.

## Understand it

Security is not a feature you add at the end; it is a set of habits.

**1. Keep secrets out of code.** Your database password must never be in a file you commit. Put it in a `.env` file, read it with `process.env`, and add `.env` to `.gitignore` before your first commit:

```
# .env  (never committed)
MONGODB_URI=mongodb+srv://user:password@cluster…
```

Bots scan GitHub for leaked keys within minutes. If a secret is ever committed, deleting it is not enough — change it, because the old one is in the history.

**2. Never trust input.** Check type, length and format of everything on the server, even if the browser already checked. Use the database library's own methods; never build a query by pasting user text into it.

**3. Never store passwords.** Store a **hash** — a one-way scrambled version made by a slow algorithm such as bcrypt or argon2. At login you hash what was typed and compare. If the database leaks, the passwords do not.

**4. Send less.** Return only the fields the client needs; never send password hashes or other people's details. And keep packages up to date: `npm audit` lists known holes.

## Key words

- **Environment variable:** a setting given to a program from outside its code, used for secrets
- **.gitignore:** the list of files Git must never commit
- **Hashing:** a one-way transformation used to store passwords safely
- **Injection:** an attack that sneaks commands in through user input

## What to do

- Deploy your API to a free Node host (for example Render)
- Set your environment variables there
- Point your front end at the live API

## Understand it

Deploying means running your server on a computer that is always on and reachable from the internet. A typical free Node host works like this:

1. Push your code to GitHub (without `.env` and `node_modules`).
2. Create a new **web service** on the host and connect the repository.
3. Set the **build command** (`npm install`) and the **start command** (`node server.js`).
4. Add your **environment variables** — such as `MONGODB_URI` — in the host's settings, not in the code.
5. Deploy. The host gives you an address like `https://task-api.onrender.com`.

One change to your code first: the host decides the port, so listen on what it gives you:

```js
const PORT = process.env.PORT || 3000;
app.listen(PORT);
```

In MongoDB Atlas, allow the host to connect (Network Access). Then point your front end's `fetch` calls at the live address.

If the front end lives on a different address from the API, the browser blocks the calls unless the server allows it — this is **CORS**. Allow only your own front end's address, not everyone. Free hosts often sleep after inactivity, so the first request can take 30 seconds: show a loading state.

## Key words

- **Deployment:** putting software on a server where people can use it
- **Build / start command:** what the host runs to prepare and launch your app
- **process.env.PORT:** the port number the host gives your server
- **CORS:** the browser rule that controls which sites may call an API

2. The database connection, with the URI in `.env`.
3. One model, with its schema and validation.
4. The routes for that model, one at a time: list, create, read one, update, delete.
5. **Test each route** the moment it is written — good data, bad data, missing id — before writing the next.

If your app has more than one kind of data (books *and* reviews), finish the first completely before starting the second.

Commit after each working step, with messages that tell the story: *Add Book model with validation*, *Add create and list book routes*, *Return 404 for unknown book id*. Your commit history is part of your portfolio — employers read it.

When something breaks, return to the debugging method: read the whole error, reproduce it, log the values, change one thing at a time. And keep a short **log** of problems you solved and how — it is the best revision notes you will ever have.

## Key words

- **Health check:** a simple route that confirms the server is running
- **Incremental development:** building and testing in small working steps
- **Commit history:** the record of every change, read like a story of the project

## What to do

- Test everything, including bad input
- Deploy the API and the front end
- Write a README explaining what it does and how to run it
- **With an AI assistant —** use it to review your code for readability (names, comments, repetition). Decide which suggestions to keep and note why; the work must stay yours.

## Understand it

"Finished" means somebody else can use it, and somebody else can run it.

**Test like a stranger.** Go through every user story from your plan on a real phone and with the keyboard only. Then try to break it: empty fields, very long text, double-tapping buttons, using it on a slow connection (DevTools → Network → Slow 4G), refreshing in the middle of an action.

**Deploy both halves** — the API on your Node host with its environment variables, the front end on GitHub Pages (or served by Express) — and test the *live* version, not your local one. Things that work on localhost often fail live: a wrong URL, a missing environment variable, CORS.

**Write the README.** It is the front door of your project. Include:

- what the app does and who it is for, with a screenshot
- the live link
- the technology used
- how to run it locally: clone, `npm install`, create `.env` with these variables, `npm start`
- what you would add next

A project with a clear README and a working link is something you can show anybody — a teacher, a scholarship panel, an employer — and they will understand it in a minute.

## Key words

- **README:** the document that explains a project and how to run it
- **Production:** the live version real users use

## What to do

- Make a portfolio page linking your three projects and capstone
- Write two or three sentences about each

## Understand it

A **portfolio** is how you show what you can do. For a developer that means working things, not claims.

Build a simple, fast portfolio page — your own HTML and CSS, published on GitHub Pages:

- **A short introduction** — your first name, what you build, what you are learning next. Keep personal details private: no home address, school or phone number.
- **Your best three or four projects**, best first. For each: a screenshot, a live link, a link to the code, and two or three sentences — what it does, what you built yourself, and one problem you solved. "I fixed a bug where the balance showed NaN by validating amounts on the server" says more than "I know JavaScript".
- **A way to get in touch** that is safe — a contact form or a GitHub profile.

Then look back honestly. Open your first page from week 1 next to your capstone. Write down three things you can do now that you could not then, and one thing you would build differently.

Keep the portfolio alive: every good project from now on goes on it. Quality over quantity — three projects you can explain fully beat ten tutorial copies.

## Key words

- **Portfolio:** a collection of your best work, shown with explanation
- **Case study:** a short account of what you built, why and how
- **Reflection:** looking back at your work to learn from it

## What to do

- Prepare a three-minute demo
- Present, and give feedback to two others

## Understand it

Presenting your work is part of the work. In three minutes, the audience should understand the problem, see the solution working, and hear one thing you learnt.

A simple structure:

1. **The problem (30 seconds).** Who has it and why it matters. "Our book club loses track of who has which book."
2. **The demo (90 seconds).** Show the app doing its main job, live. Use real-looking data prepared beforehand. Follow a story: add a book, lend it, return it.
3. **How you built it (40 seconds).** The stack in one sentence, and one hard problem you solved.
4. **What is next (20 seconds).** One or two features you would add.

Rehearse it twice out loud with a timer. Have a **backup** — screenshots or a recording — because live demos fail at the worst moment and the Wi-Fi will not care that it is your turn.

When giving feedback to others, be kind and specific: one thing that works well and why, and one concrete suggestion. "The search is fast and I liked that it ignores capitals; maybe show how many results were found" helps. "Nice" does not.

## Key words

- **Demo:** showing software working, live
- **Elevator pitch:** a very short explanation of what something is and why it matters
- **Constructive feedback:** specific, kind comments that help someone improve
